newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - Low-delta yen puts bid despite time decay.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Low-delta yen puts bid despite time decay.

text.p: Out-of-the-money yen puts in dollar/yen stayed resilient in the U.S., despite the time-decay concerns enveloping the market, as the dollar rose to striking distance of the 125 yen barrier, dealers said.

Although trading had been slow so far today, a break of the 124.82-yen February high could probably lead to a spike above 125.00 yen, where a lot of exotic option barriers have piled up during the recent range trading, they said.
"There's been so much talk about triggers above 125 that people are trying to catch some gamma on the upside," said a U.S. bank trader in California.

"That's why 126 (yen) puts in the two-weeks were so well bid overnight," he added. Shorter-dated options have higher gamma, which gives them quicker price acceleration when spot moves but also makes them vulnerable to time decay.

When a big exotic option barrier price is broken, banks that had been selling short-dated vanilla options to hedge theta decay of their exotic option sales to end-users must scramble to cover the vanillas, adding fuel to the spot move.
"A higher dollar, out of the range, is going to mean volatility," said Alan Revercomb, options strategist at I.D.E.A. Inc.

Still, the California trader added that interest appeared limited to the low-deltas as time decay had become the market's primary concern after Tuesday's Federal Reserve credit tightening and ahead of the Easter weekend, they said.
"People are willing to get some gamma if the dollar is going to break above 125, but they're not interested in paying time decay for the levels that we're at right now," he said.
At-the-money options have the steepest time decay because their premiums consist only of time value and are also higher than out-of-the-money option premiums in dollar terms.
Standard at-the-money one-week dollar/yen volatility stood at 9.7/10.7 percent late in the U.S. morning business, down from 10.0/11.0 late on Tuesday.
One-month volatility stood at 10.1/10.4 percent, unchanged from late Tuesday levels after the U.S. rate hike, but off nearly half a point from early Tuesday levels.
Risk reversals, the put/call pricing differential, widened their skew toward yen puts. One-month 25-delta was assessed at 0.2/0.4 point in favor of yen puts against 0.1/0.3 on Tuesday.
The dollar was off overnight highs near 124.50 yen but was still hovering above 124.00 yen in the U.S.
By comparison, dollar/mark volatilities were simply crushed by time-decay as the spot drifted near the middle of recent ranges, mostly in the 1.6900-1.6950 mark area.

"Tomorrow's probably going to be already limited in terms of liquidity, and Friday and Monday are going to be dead," the California trader said. Most U.S. traders will take Friday off, and most European traders are off Friday and Monday for Easter.
One-week dollar/mark volatility fell nearly 1.5 point from late Tuesday levels to 7.7/8.7 percent, and one-month lost almost a full point to 8.9/9.1 percent.
